rationale: Axioms (V1)-(V5) carry exactly the content of Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right 4e, 1.20 (commutativity, associativity of + and of scalars, additive identity, additive inverse, 1v=v, both distributive properties), repackaged as 'the additive structure is an abelian group' plus four scalar axioms. That repackaging is itself the source's: Wikipedia's Vector space states 'The first four axioms (related to vector addition) say that a vector space is an abelian group under addition.' Convention deltas: the zero vector 0_V is part of the data here, where Axler 1.20 asserts only that some additive identity exists; scalar multiplication is explicitly typed F x V -> V and the item warns it is not a binary operation on a set. Statement is a faithful repackaging of a located source, not an invention. Definition carries no proof section; its notation-legitimacy argument only cites lem-identity-unique and lem-inverse-unique, so proof is not-applicable. The Remark's independence witness for (V5) (set lambda*v := 0_V on any abelian group) is a standard checkable observation, verified inline.

Claim 1 is Axler 4e 1.30 ('0v = 0 for every v in V'), claim 2 is 1.31 ('a0 = 0 for every a in F'), claim 4 is 1.32 ('(-1)v = -v for every v in V'), claim 5 is Exercise 1B.2 ('Suppose a in F, v in V, and av = 0. Prove that a = 0 or v = 0'). Claim 3 ((-lambda)v = -(lambda v) and lambda(-v) = -(lambda v)) is the standard companion, obtained by the same two-readings-and-cancel argument. Five located sourced results merged into one lemma, so ai-altered rather than literature-derived. Proof adapts Axler's own arguments (write one element two ways, then cancel) to the library's group-cancellation lemma and its uniqueness-of-inverses lemma, hence ai-altered rather than locally invented.

F^X with the pointwise operations is Axler 4e 1.24-1.25 (notation F^S, (f+g)(x) = f(x)+g(x), (lambda f)(x) = lambda f(x), zero the constant function at 0) and Wikipedia's Function space ('(f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x), (c.f)(x)=c.f(x)'). Convention deltas, all recorded in the item: Axler 1.25 requires S nonempty, whereas here X is arbitrary so that F^0 = F^(empty set) is a genuine case and is the one-point zero space; Axler reads F^n as F^{1,...,n}, whereas here X = n is the von Neumann natural {0,...,n-1} so coordinates are indexed from 0. Proof component is the pointwise verification of (V1)-(V5) that Axler 1.25 leaves to the reader, written out here; adapted rather than invented.

An m-by-n matrix over F with entrywise addition and scalar multiplication is standard (Wikipedia, Matrix (mathematics): 'Matrix addition and subtraction ... are calculated entrywise'; 'The product cA of a number c and a matrix A is computed by multiplying each entry of A by c'), and Examples of vector spaces lists the matrix space. Realising it as the function space F^(m x n), so that the vector-space structure is inherited with no second verification, is a formalisation choice, as is indexing both i and j from 0. The degenerate 0-by-n and m-by-0 shapes correspond to Wikipedia's 'empty matrix'. No proof is supplied here: the item explicitly defers all verification to def-function-space, hence not-applicable.

Claim 2 is Wikipedia's Restriction of scalars specialised from a ring homomorphism to a subfield inclusion: 'Suppose that M is a module over S. Then it can be regarded as a module over R where the action of R is given via M x R -> M, (m,r) -> m . f(r)'. Claim 1 (a field is a vector space over itself) and claim 3 (a field is a vector space over each of its subfields) are the standard field-extension examples on Wikipedia's Vector space. Merged and specialised, hence ai-altered. The axiom-by-axiom verification, including the explicit accounting in the Remark of which unrestricted field axioms are spent in steps 1.4-1.6, is written locally.

(W1), (W2), (W3) are Axler 4e 1.34 verbatim in content: 'additive identity 0 in U; closed under addition u,w in U implies u+w in U; closed under scalar multiplication a in F and u in U implies au in U'. Taking these three as the definition rather than as a characterisation of Axler 1.33 changes nothing, since 1.34 is an if-and-only-if. The name 'linear subspace' is the Wikipedia article title and Axler's noted synonym ('Some people use the terminology linear subspace, which means the same as subspace'). Remark 3 is Axler's own margin note that (W1) may be replaced by nonemptiness given (W3). Proof component is the in-body argument that W with the restricted operations is a vector space, which follows Axler's proof of 1.34 (including deriving -u = (-1)u from 1.32) adapted to the library's items.

The statement is the conjunction of located sourced facts, merged without changing content: Axler 4e 1.34 gives the three subspace conditions and 1.32 gives (-1)v = -v; Wikipedia's Subgroup gives the subgroup conditions ('for every a and b in H, the product ab is in H'; 'for every a in H, the inverse a^-1 is in H', with the identity in H). Their conjunction is the standard submodule characterisation, 'the linear subspaces of V are exactly the subgroups of its additive group that are closed under scalar multiplication'. Not located as one sourced sentence, so ai-altered with semantic sources rather than literature-derived. The two-direction proof is written locally.

Wikipedia's Linear subspace gives the one-step test on a nonempty W: 'whenever w1, w2 are elements of W and alpha, beta are elements of K, it follows that alpha w1 + beta w2 is in W'. The library uses the equivalent single-scalar form lambda u + v in W; that is the only content delta, and the item proves the equivalence with the three conditions of def-linear-subspace (Axler 1.34). The explicit warning that nonemptiness cannot be dropped matches Axler's margin note on 1.34. Proof, including the deliberate ordering (0_V before closure under scalars), is written locally.

Axler 4e Exercise 1C.11: 'Prove that the intersection of every collection of subspaces of V is a subspace of V'; Wikipedia's Linear subspace: 'Given subspaces U and W of a vector space V, then their intersection U intersect W is also a subspace of V'. Content delta, recorded in the item: the library requires the family to be nonempty, because the intersection of the empty family of subsets of V is not a subset of V under this library's conventions, whereas Axler's ambient-space convention would make it V. That is a specialisation, not a change of content. Proof written locally via the one-step test.

Wikipedia's Linear span gives both descriptions the item uses: 'the smallest linear subspace of V that contains S', 'the intersection of all linear subspaces that contain S', and 'the set of all finite linear combinations of the elements of S'. The library takes the intersection form as the definition, exactly as it does for def-generated-subgroup. Axler 4e 2.2/2.4 give the linear-combination and span definitions for a finite list. Convention deltas: a linear combination is indexed by a von Neumann natural n and the finite sum is the library's monoid finite product, so the empty combination is a genuine case rather than the source's stipulated convention; span is defined for an arbitrary subset, not a finite list. Proof component is the short well-definedness argument (the family of subspaces containing S is nonempty because V is one, so lem-intersection-of-linear-subspaces applies) plus the uniqueness argument for the definite article, both adapted from the standard route.

The equality of the outside and inside descriptions of the span is asserted by Wikipedia's Linear span (span(S) is both 'the intersection of all linear subspaces that contain S' and 'the set of all finite linear combinations of the elements of S'), and Axler 4e 2.6 proves 'the span of a list of vectors in V is the smallest subspace of V containing all vectors in the list'. Content delta, and the reason the item exists: Wikipedia and Axler 2.4 stipulate span(empty) = {0}, whereas here it is derived from the empty sum of def-monoid-finite-product. Proof is written locally: two inductions over the library's finite-sum recursion (scalars pass through a finite sum; a subspace containing S contains every combination) plus an explicit list-extension lemma at step 1.3.

Wikipedia's Closure operator states the three properties verbatim ('X is a subset of cl(X)', 'X subset of Y implies cl(X) subset of cl(Y)', 'cl(cl(X)) = cl(X)') and names 'the function that associates to every subset of a given vector space its linear span' as an example, with the closed sets the linear subspaces; that is claims 1-4. Claim 5 (span(S union {0_V}) = span(S)) is an added easy consequence of claims 1-2 and (W1), not a separate sourced result, and is directly checkable. Merged and extended, hence ai-altered. Proof written locally from the defining minimality of the span.

Claim 1 is Axler 4e 2.4 at a one-element list: 'span(v1,...,vm) = {a1 v1 + ... + am vm : a1,...,am in F}', which at m = 1 is span(v) = {av : a in F}. Claim 2 is the immediate degenerate case. Claim 3 (for v nonzero, lambda v = mu v forces lambda = mu) is the standard consequence of Axler Exercise 1B.2 (av = 0 implies a = 0 or v = 0) and (V3). Merged, hence ai-altered. Proof written locally via the one-step test.

Axler 4e 1.36 defines the sum verbatim in content: 'V1 + ... + Vm = {v1 + ... + vm : v1 in V1, ..., vm in Vm}', and 1.40 records that it is a subspace. Convention delta, recorded in the item: the family is indexed by the von Neumann natural n, so n = 0 is a genuine case and the empty sum of subspaces is {0_V}, which Axler's 1,...,m indexing excludes; U + W is derived as the case n = 2 rather than defined separately. The three auxiliary facts (F1) all-zero list sums to 0_V, (F2) the mixed identity, (F3) extracting one term by replacing it with 0_V, are local bookkeeping forced by that indexing choice and are proved inline by induction; the proof component is therefore locally written.

Axler 4e 1.40: 'Suppose V1, ..., Vm are subspaces of V. Then V1 + ... + Vm is the smallest subspace of V containing V1, ..., Vm.' The item restates that minimality as the identity sum(U_i) = span(union U_i), which is equivalent given Wikipedia's characterisation of the span as the smallest linear subspace containing a set; the item also states the minimality form explicitly. Reformulated, hence ai-altered. Proof written locally, including the induction that a linear subspace is closed under the library's finite sums.

(D2) is the Encyclopedia of Mathematics condition (c) for an internal direct sum: 'the intersection of G_i with the Omega-subgroup generated by the remaining ideals is the trivial subgroup', with (D1) its condition (a) that the summands generate. Axler 4e 1.46 gives the two-summand form the item derives ('U + W is a direct sum if and only if U intersect W = {0}'), and Axler's remark after 1.46 states the very warning the item makes: 'When asking about a possible direct sum with more than two subspaces, it is not enough to test that each pair of the subspaces intersect only at 0.' Wikipedia's internal direct sum ('If every x in M can be written in exactly one way as a sum of finitely many elements of the M_i') is the equivalent form proved in lem-direct-sum-criterion. Deltas: the sum of the other summands is realised by replacing the j-th summand with {0_V} rather than re-indexing over a smaller set, and the empty family is a genuine case with V = the zero space. Local proofs (that {0_V} is a subspace, that (D2) implies pairwise triviality, the two-summand reduction, the empty case).

Condition (b) is Axler 4e 1.41's definition of a direct sum ('each element of V1 + ... + Vm can be written in only one way as a sum v1 + ... + vm, where each vk in Vk') together with the sum being all of V; (b) if and only if (c) is Axler 1.45 ('V1 + ... + Vm is a direct sum if and only if the only way to write 0 as a sum v1 + ... + vm, where each vk in Vk, is by taking each vk equal to 0'); (a) if and only if (b) is the standard equivalence with the Encyclopedia of Mathematics intersection condition, and Wikipedia's internal direct sum is stated in form (b). Three located sourced statements merged into one three-way equivalence, hence ai-altered. Proof written locally.

R as a vector space over itself and over Q is the standard field-extension example on Wikipedia's Vector space; the action q.x := iota(q)x of claim 3 is exactly Wikipedia's restriction of scalars along a ring homomorphism, '(m,r) -> m . f(r)', with f = iota. Construction delta, forced by this library and recorded in the item: Q is not a subset of this library's R (a rational is a class of pairs of integers, a real a class of Cauchy sequences of rationals), so the item works with the subfield iota[Q] for claim 2 and proves claim 3 about Q itself directly rather than by restriction of scalars. Verification written locally.

Axler 4e Example 1.43 is exactly this construction: 'Suppose Vk is the subspace of F^n of those vectors whose coordinates are all 0, except possibly in the kth slot ... Then F^n = V1 (+) ... (+) Vn.' The item is that example written out at n = 3 with the library's 0-based von Neumann indexing (L_0, L_1, L_2 and e_0, e_1, e_2), together with the identification L_j = span{e_j} and the F^0 boundary case (Axler's F^n is stated for positive n). Specialised and reindexed, hence ai-altered. Verification written locally.

Wikipedia's Sequence space: 'The space of eventually zero sequences, c00, is the subspace of c0 consisting of all sequences which have only finitely many nonzero elements', and identifies the standard unit sequences e_i ('the sequence which is zero but for a 1 in the ith entry'); Examples of vector spaces gives the finitely-supported sequence space as a vector space over F. Axler 4e 1.23 gives F^infinity, the space of all sequences over F, with pointwise operations. Deltas: stated over an arbitrary field with no order, norm or topology, indexed from 0, and E is identified as the span of the e_k rather than assumed to be. Claim 3 (the constant family at 1_F lies outside E) is the standard witness that the span of an infinite set uses only finite combinations. Verification written locally, including the induction computing the partial sums.

The construction is located verbatim in Margalit and Rabinoff, Interactive Linear Algebra 2.6, Example: 'The first quadrant in R^2 is not a subspace. It contains the origin and is closed under addition, but it is not closed under scalar multiplication (by negative numbers).' The item recasts that example as the refutation of the general false claim 'contains 0_V and closed under addition implies linear subspace', names the witness e_0 = (1,0) and pins the failure to the single scalar -1, and additionally observes that Q is therefore not even a subgroup of the additive group. Reformulated and sharpened, hence ai-altered. Verification written locally from the ordered-field axioms of this library's R.

The construction is the standard one and is located: Andrea Minini, The union of vector subspaces, states of the union of two subspaces that 'It is only closed under scalar multiplication' while 'the union A union B is not closed under addition', using exactly the x-axis and y-axis of R^2 and the witness (1,0) + (0,1) = (1,1). Axler 4e Exercise 1C.8 asks for precisely this object: 'Give an example of a nonempty subset U of R^2 such that U is closed under scalar multiplication, but U is not a subspace of R^2.' Delta: the item states the witness over an arbitrary field F, using only 1_F != 0_F, instead of over R, and phrases it as the refutation of the converse false claim. Verification written locally.

ALPHA ESCALATION (evidence class needs concurrence). The proposition being witnessed is sourced: Axler 4e, remark after 1.46, 'When asking about a possible direct sum with more than two subspaces, it is not enough to test that each pair of the subspaces intersect only at 0', with Example 1.44 as its witness (three subspaces of F^3, pairwise intersections all {0}, sum all of F^3, decompositions not unique). No source was located for THIS witness, the three lines span{e_0}, span{e_1}, span{e_0 + e_1} in F^2. It is not an invention: it is the standard minimal separation (three distinct lines through the origin of a plane), it is recoverable directly from the sourced proposition by taking the smallest ambient space, and it is fully checkable in the two displayed decompositions of d. Recorded as ai-altered under the established-knowledge waiver rather than ai-generated; falls back to ai-generated if Alpha does not concur. Verification written locally.

ALPHA ESCALATION (evidence class needs concurrence). The pair of coordinate hyperplanes U = {x : x_2 = 0} and W = {x : x_0 = 0} of F^3, with U + W = F^3 and U intersect W = span{e_1} so that the sum is not direct, is the standard 'a sum can be everything without being direct' computation; Axler 4e Examples 1.37, 1.42 and 1.44 are the same genus over F^3 (coordinate subspaces, their sums, and a non-direct sum), but no source was located for this exact pair of subspaces. It is a recoverable specialisation of established material, not an invented claim, and every assertion is verified by explicit coordinate computation in the item. Recorded as ai-altered under the established-knowledge waiver rather than ai-generated; falls back to ai-generated if Alpha does not concur. Verification written locally.

The false claim and the exact condition in the Remarks are Axler 4e Exercise 1C.12 verbatim: 'Prove that the union of two subspaces of V is a subspace of V if and only if one of the subspaces is contained in the other', together with Axler's margin note 'The union of subspaces is rarely a subspace (see Exercise 12)'. The refuting construction, the two coordinate axes of the plane with (1,0) + (0,1) = (1,1) outside their union, is located in Andrea Minini, The union of vector subspaces. Delta: stated over an arbitrary field rather than R, and packaged as a false-statement item with the criterion moved to the Remarks. Refutation written locally.
